Summary Malaysia Airports Holdings Bhd (MAHB) is in negotiations with AirAsia Group Bhd to establish a structured repayment plan for RM500 million in outstanding debt, as reported by Bloomberg.
 MAHB's managing director, Datuk Mohd Izani Ghani, affirmed that discussions have been progressing well, emphasizing the need to balance debt recovery with maintaining essential connectivity provided by AirAsia.
 This financial challenge for AirAsia is compounded by rising jet fuel costs due to Middle Eastern conflicts, contributing to a significant 73% decline in its stock value this year.
 The information was revealed in a report by the Public Accounts Committee.
 Make Malay Mail your preferred source on Google Giving you news that matter to Malaysians. Make Malay Mail your preferred source when you search for news on Google. By Malay Mail First Published: Tuesday, 17 Nov 2026 10:29 AM MYT × Subscribe to Newsletter
 Subscribe KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 17 — Airport operator Malaysia Airports Holdings Bhd (MAHB) is negotiating a structured repayment plan with AirAsia Group Bhd to recover RM500 million in outstanding debt owed by the budget carrier, according to Bloomberg .
 Bilateral negotiations “have been progressing well over the past couple months,” MAHB managing director Datuk Mohd Izani Ghani informed lawmakers during committee hearings last month.
 “Our priority is to ensure that the debt is settled,” he said, noting that while the airport operator remains focused on recovering its receivables, management is mindful that the low-cost carrier “provides essential connectivity to Malaysians.”
 Izani’s testimony was disclosed in a report tabled by the bipartisan Public Accounts Committee (PAC), the parliamentary watchdog tasked with scrutinising federal accounts and public expenditure.
 The debt overhang arrives as AirAsia navigates severe operational turbulence.
 Operating without fuel hedges, the budget carrier has absorbed punishing cost spikes as regional conflict in the Middle East drove global jet fuel prices higher, triggering a steep sell-off that has battered its stock by 73 per cent this year.
